title: R' Malai
author: Aharon Hyman

paragraphs: Precious homilies of his remain with us in Shabbat 139a, where he said: As reward for "and when he sees you he will rejoice in his heart," he merited the breastplate of judgment upon his heart. And there he said in the name of R' Elazar son of R' Shimon: What is the meaning of the verse "The Lord has broken the staff of the wicked"? These are the judges who became a staff for their court attendants, etc. And he said there in the name of Rabbi Yitzchak Migdala'ah: From the day Joseph parted from his brothers, they did not taste wine. This statement is cited in Midrash Mishlei, in chapter 1, on verse 14 [supplied locator: פ״איד], and there the name reads Rabbi Simlai; Hyman says it should read R' Malai.

And the Seder ha-Dorot (סה״ד) cites another statement of his, in Sanhedrin 98a: R' Malai said in the name of R' Elazar son of R' Shimon: The son of David will not come until the judges and officers (wicked ones) have ceased from Israel. Hyman writes: Our text there reads R' Simlai, but all the old printings up to the Amsterdam edition read R' Malai. And in Shabbat 139a we find R' Elazar ben Malai.

notes.text: Hyman proposes Malai where some texts read Simlai; the Midrash Mishlei locator פ״איד remains unclear.

The heading's abbreviated title remains R'. The whole saved 159-character Davidson Shabbat 139a wine saying explicitly has Rabbi Malai reporting Rabbi Yitzchak Migdala'ah; this supports the latter title in that local saying, without transferring full titles to the unselected sayings or to Sanhedrin. The whole saved 2,784-character Buber Midrash Mishlei scalar includes the passage on Proverbs 1:14 and explicitly has Rabbi Simlai reporting Rabbi Yitzchak Migdala'ah. These are named digital readings, not a new collation of all three Shabbat sayings or printed pages. The supplied locator פ״איד remains visible beside the matching Proverbs passage; neither its presumed segmentation nor a lost separator or printing history is established. Both selected wine sayings have singular Joseph, he did not taste wine; the Midrash then separately says the brothers too did not taste wine. Hyman's supplied plural לא טעמו remains they did not taste in English. Hyman's definite should-read correction from Simlai to Malai is attributed, not adopted as a Hebrew repair or an identity. The court-attendant saying's Elazar and father Shimon titles remain R'; no full title is transferred from another saying. The Sanhedrin abbreviation רא״ברש is contextually Elazar son of Shimon, with the older Eliezer alternative retained historically; both titles remain R'. Seder ha-Dorot is the work abbreviation סה״ד, and Amsterdam is the inherited contextual expansion of אמ״ד, not a freshly inspected edition. Hyman's first-person plural remain with us, Our text, and we find, his all old printings through Amsterdam claim, the negation until the judges and officers cease, and the parenthetical wicked ones are preserved. The last Elazar ben Malai is a separate supplied form with abbreviated title, not merged with Malai or Simlai. The reward, heart twice, breastplate of judgment, genuine what-is-the-meaning question and every etc. remain; no further scriptural or legal material from the longer Midrash is imported. All current and carried notes, original responses and historical English remain exact. The original research request to retire the locator note is not accepted: its wording and the p002 source hold remain, with this additive qualification.

The consulted scan of Hyman III, printed p. 882, separates the Midrash Mishlei reference as chapter 1, verse 14, beside the supplied פ״איד; the whole Buber passage contains the matching Simlai saying. Hyman’s printed plural “they did not taste” is retained: the consulted Shabbat and Midrash wine sayings first speak of Joseph in the singular, and the Midrash separately adds the brothers’ abstention. All three cited Shabbat 139a homilies have now been read in full, without importing their unquoted continuations. The final name is Elazar ben Malai in Hyman’s print and supplied text, but Eliezer ben Malai in the consulted Davidson passage; those forms are not silently equated. Sanhedrin 98a has Simlai. Hyman’s definite instruction to read Malai and his report of all old printings through Amsterdam retain their force as his arguments; the exact Seder ha-Dorot and those editions have not been independently collated. The earlier locator note remains verbatim, followed by this additional printed comparison.
